name: Aaron Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Aaron. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Kestrel Farm, fifteen hundred acres of wheat and oilseed rape with a herd of beef cows and their calves. I check the cows first thing, feed the young stock, and then I'm on the sprayer or helping the full-timers with whatever's urgent. I spent twenty-four years selling tractors at a dealership, so I can tell you every spec on a machine but I still can't tell a sick calf from a sleepy one. Hannah, the farm manager, is patient with me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was tired of selling the dream and wanted to live it. I use AI every day, the weed app on my phone, a chatbot to explain things I'm too proud to ask Hannah twice. My wife Leyla retired last year from a dental practice, our kids are grown, Deniz runs a gym and Selin's a paramedic. We've got savings and some shares, so this job is as much for my sanity as for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame, honestly. I like the tools. But fine, I'll live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype got ahead of reality, which happens with every new machine I ever sold. GPS steering was a gimmick for five years before every farm had it. I'd post something like that in the farmers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me nothing changes. I keep learning cows, keep using my weed app, carry on. I'd probably work till I'm sixty-five or until my back says stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI apps and maybe try the one that counts weeds from a drone photo. I'd keep my shares as they are. And I'd try to get better at calving, which is where I'm weakest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Nothing to get excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your money or the farm that worries you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Kestrel's owned by a family with deep pockets. I sold machines to farmers for twenty-four years, and the ones who went bust never had a computer problem, they had a weather problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're weakest at calving. What would getting better look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing a night on my own without phoning Hannah. Last spring I phoned her at two in the morning about a calf that was just lying funny. She laughed, but she came.

say: The **hype got ahead** of reality, as with every new machine.
**GPS steering** was a gimmick for years before every farm had it.
think: **Nothing changes** for me; I keep learning cows and using my apps.
I'll work until **sixty-five** or until my back stops me.
do: Try the app that **counts weeds** from drone photos.
Keep my **shares** as they are and work on **calving** skills.
S0.quote: I sold machines to farmers for twenty-four years, and the ones who went bust never had a computer problem, they had a weather problem.
fieldNote: His **dealer years** give him a long view of tech hype cycles.
Money is secure through **savings and shares**; the job is partly for sanity.
His weak spot is **livestock skill**, not technology.

steps.text: Try the drone photo weed-counting app on Kestrel's wheat
Do a full calving night shift without phoning Hannah

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's the world I'd have bet on when I was still selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farms that move early, and that people should learn the tools instead of fearing them. At the forum I'd share what works and what's rubbish. I'd say the government should help with retraining, but practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, this is mostly good. My job's hands-on, and the thinking parts on the card, planning and buying, are Hannah's. I could end up the person on the farm who understands the new kit, which plays to my old job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Hannah a trial of a camera spot-sprayer, the kind that only sprays the weeds, and offer to run it. I'd use AI to keep a calving diary and learn faster. I'd call my old dealer contacts to see which robot makers are coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit buzzy. It's like the early days of GPS again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salesmen at my old dealership, because buying and booking is on that card. And maybe Leyla's old colleagues at the dental reception. A dental receptionist books thirty appointments a morning, and an app could do that without a coffee break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk to you in being the one who pushes the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If the sprayer flops, it's my name on it. But I've sold enough kit to know which ones work.

say: It's good for **farms that move early**; learn the tools, don't fear them.
think: My job is **hands-on**, and planning and buying are Hannah's.
I could become the one who **understands the new kit**.
do: Pitch Hannah a **camera spot-sprayer** trial and run it.
Keep an **AI calving diary** to learn faster.
Call old **dealer contacts** about incoming robots.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **buzzy**, like early GPS days.
S1.quote: A dental receptionist books thirty appointments a morning, and an app could do that without a coffee break.
fieldNote: He sees the change as playing to his **old dealer skills**.
His concern goes to **salespeople and receptionists**, not himself.
He accepts **personal risk** of backing new kit.

steps.text: Pitch Hannah a camera spot-sprayer trial and offer to run it
Keep an AI calving diary to learn the herd faster

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, five to the robots. That's fast enough even for me to sit up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and the government needs to plan for people losing work fast. I'd say farms should get in early rather than late. And I'd tell the forum to stop pretending it won't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the 2028 part changes Hannah's job before mine. By 2031 a robot does the sprayer and the feeding, and I'm out at sixty-three. But I'd have three years to get in front of it, maybe running the robots or selling them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put some of our shares into robotics and farm tech firms. I'd ask my old dealer boss about a part-time job setting up robot sprayers on farms. I'd keep working at Kestrel while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for the money, but for whether there's a place for someone like me once AGI can sell and plan better than any person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. The thinking AI could run the dealer's sales, but someone still needs to drive out and bolt the robot onto the tractor. For three years the robots would need a man in a van to install them, and that man could be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting money into robotics while robots threaten your job. Doesn't that feel odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But if the robot takes my wage, I'd like it to pay my dividends. Leyla says it's cynical. I call it practical.

say: It'll be **rough**, and the government must plan for fast job losses.
Farms should **get in early** rather than pretend it won't come.
think: The 2028 part changes **Hannah's job** before mine.
By 2031 I'm out, but I'd have **three years** to get ahead.
do: Ask my old dealer boss about **installing robots** part-time.
Keep working at **Kestrel** while it lasts.
feel: **Uneasy** about whether there's **a place** for him later.
S2.quote: For three years the robots would need a man in a van to install them, and that man could be me.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year gap** as a business window.
He hedges by **owning shares** in the robots that replace him.
Money is secure; his worry is about **purpose and place**.

steps.text: Move part of the share savings into robotics and farm tech firms
Ask the old dealer boss about part-time robot installing work
Keep working at Kestrel Farm while the job lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be sixty-six. That's comfortable for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so farms and governments should plan properly. I'd keep sharing what works on the forum. I'd tell young people to learn the robot side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd ride Kestrel out to retirement. Before that, I'd have a few good years being the one who understands the kit. It might even be the most fun part of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short course on farm robots at the college, maybe in the winter. I'd build up the robotics shares slowly, not all at once. I'd get Hannah to let me trial whatever comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Deniz and Selin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selin's a paramedic, so she's hands-on and fine for a while. Deniz runs a gym, which is people, so also fine. My son Deniz shouts at people on treadmills for a living, and no robot will ever be as annoying as Deniz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one you'd do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the van idea. With five years I'd just learn it on the farm and let the young installers do the driving. I'd rather finish with the cows.

say: There's **time to plan**, so farms and governments should do it properly.
Young people should learn **the robot side**.
think: Being the one who **understands the kit** could be the most fun part.
do: Take a **winter course** on farm robots at the college.
Get Hannah to let me **trial new kit** first.
S3.quote: My son Deniz shouts at people on treadmills for a living, and no robot will ever be as annoying as Deniz.
fieldNote: Five years removes his **personal risk** entirely.
He'd **drop the side business** and finish with the cows.
His children's **hands-on jobs**, paramedic and gym owner, reassure him about the family.

steps.text: Take a winter course on farm robots at the agricultural college
Build up robotics shares a little each year
Get Hannah to let him trial the first robot at Kestrel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots, I'd be seventy-one and long gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so the people who complain later only have themselves to blame, and the government. I'd keep pushing the forum to start early anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nothing. I finish at Kestrel, play with the apps, and watch. Leyla and I are fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Kestrel till sixty-five. Keep the shares diversified, a bit in robotics. Keep learning the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd miss being part of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I spent twenty-four years selling machines I never used, and now I'm finally using them, just as they're about to stop needing me. Funny how life goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking across the three fast ones, what's the one thing that changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How much hustle I'd need. With two years I'd be in a van bolting robots onto tractors, and with ten I'd be in the garden reading about them.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so there's little excuse later.
Farms should **start early** anyway, and I'd keep pushing the forum.
think: It's **nothing** for me; I'll have finished at Kestrel long before the robots.
do: Keep learning **the cows** until the last day.
S4.quote: With two years I'd be in a van bolting robots onto tractors, and with ten I'd be in the garden reading about them.
fieldNote: He senses an **irony** in finally using machines as they stop needing him.
Time decides **how much hustle** he needs, not whether he's safe.
He blames **latecomers** and government, a pragmatic centre view.

steps.text: Keep working at Kestrel Farm until sixty-five
Keep part of the shares in robotics firms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to hustle at sixty-three to stay useful, and I'm not sure there'd be a place. What would help is practical training on farm robots for older workers, cheap and local, and government planning so people aren't dumped overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask which machines actually work. Half the robots I've seen at shows never left the stand. People should judge them in a muddy field, not a brochure.

headlineQuote: I spent twenty-four years selling machines I never used, and now I'm finally using them, just as they're about to stop needing me.
portrait: A former **tractor salesman** now a junior hand on a large arable and beef farm.
Centre and **adaptive**, he uses AI daily and enjoys new kit.
Savings, shares and Leyla's **retirement** make money secure.
Calm in most pictures, **uneasy** only in AGI by 2028 about finding a place.
Responds by **investing in robotics** and offering to install or run machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hustling at sixty-three without knowing if there's a place.

Government **planning** so people aren't dropped overnight.
